opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is that in the 1980s, most AI researchers didn't really think of their systems as agents at all, at least not in any unified sense. The field had fragmented into a collection of subfields, each with its own problems, its own conferences, its own notion of what counted as success. You had people working on knowledge representation, people working on planning, on natural language, on vision, on expert systems, on machine learning, which was still quite a small community then, and they didn't talk to each other very much. Each group had a particular piece of the puzzle and tended to treat that piece as if it were the whole thing.

So if you asked a knowledge representation person what intelligence was, they'd tell you it was about having the right logical formalism and drawing the right inferences. A planning person would tell you it was about finding sequences of actions that achieve a goal, typically in a world that was fully known and deterministic, which of course the real world isn't. And the expert systems people were building rule-based systems that were, in a sense, consultants. They answered questions; they didn't act in the world.

What was missing was the overarching framework: the idea that what we're really trying to build is something that perceives its environment and acts in it, and that what makes it intelligent is that it acts in a way that can be expected to achieve its objectives given what it perceives. Once you adopt that view, a lot of things fall into place. You see that logic is one way of representing knowledge, but you also need to handle uncertainty, so probability comes in. You see that goals are too crude, and you really need utilities, so decision theory comes in. You see that planning and learning and perception aren't separate subjects; they're all components of one agent that has to work together.

And interestingly, a lot of those ideas already existed in economics, in control theory, in operations research, in statistics. AI had, to some extent, walled itself off from those fields, partly as a reaction against the more numerical, cybernetics-style approaches of the 1950s and 60s. So the 1980s were in some ways a period of intellectual isolation. Toward the end of the decade, with Judea Pearl's work on Bayesian networks and the reconnection with decision theory, that started to change.

That was really a big part of the motivation when Peter Norvig and I wrote our textbook. We wanted to present AI not as a grab bag of techniques but as a coherent field organized around the rational agent. And I think that view has largely won out. Though, as I've been arguing for some years now, it has its own deep flaw: it assumes that we can specify the objective correctly and hand it to the machine. That assumption, which seemed harmless when the systems were weak, becomes very dangerous as the systems become more capable.

r001.rationale: The response says expert systems answered questions rather than acting in the world, but does not explain that treating them solely as providers of correct answers allowed researchers to disregard their status as agents.

r002.rationale: It discusses objectives in the general rational-agent framework, but does not state that a question-answering system needs to reason about its own objectives.

r003.rationale: It does not say that giving an answer should be considered an action or that the system must account for the answer’s effects.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the honest answer is that in the 1980s, most of the field didn't really think in terms of agents at all. The dominant framing was that AI was about building components: a vision system, a planner, a knowledge base, an inference engine, a natural language parser. Each of these was a subfield with its own conferences, its own benchmarks, its own notion of what counted as progress. And the question of how these pieces would fit together into something that actually perceives the world and acts in it over time was, for the most part, deferred.

There were exceptions, of course. The planning community, going back to STRIPS and Shakey the robot, had a notion of a system that forms a plan and executes it. And the people working on expert systems were building things that gave advice, which is a kind of action. But the mental model was largely one of a system that is given a problem, thinks about it, and produces an answer. Input, computation, output. The world was assumed to be static, fully observable, and deterministic, because those assumptions made the problems tractable. And so the agent, if you want to call it that, never really had to deal with uncertainty, with the passage of time, with the consequences of its own actions coming back to bite it.

What was missing, I'd say, was the connection to decision theory and to control theory, which had been developed in neighbouring fields for decades. The economists and the statisticians had a perfectly good notion of a rational agent: something that has beliefs about the world, has preferences over outcomes, and chooses actions to maximize expected utility. The control theorists had the notion of a feedback loop, of a system that continuously observes and adjusts. AI in the 1980s was somewhat insulated from both of those traditions. There was a strong attachment to logic as the foundation, and logic doesn't have a natural place for degrees of belief or for trade-offs among goals.

Now, I don't want to be too harsh about this. The logical tradition gave us enormously important ideas about representation and reasoning. And by the late 1980s things were changing quite rapidly. Judea Pearl's work on Bayesian networks made probabilistic reasoning respectable again. People like Rod Brooks were arguing, in a very different direction, that you should start from the sensing-and-acting loop rather than from internal reasoning. And a number of us started to think that the right way to unify the field was to ask: what is the agent as a whole supposed to be doing? And the answer that emerged was essentially the decision-theoretic one. An intelligent agent is one that acts so as to achieve its objectives, given what it perceives.

That framing, which Peter Norvig and I put at the centre of our textbook in the early 1990s, turned out to be very productive. It let you see the components as serving a common purpose rather than as separate hobbies. But I'd also say, with the benefit of hindsight, that it carried a hidden assumption that has come back to trouble us. The assumption was that the objective is given. Someone hands the agent its utility function, and the agent's job is simply to optimize it. In the 1980s, and frankly for a couple of decades after, nobody worried much about where that objective comes from or what happens if it's wrong, because the systems weren't capable enough for it to matter. That's the piece of the picture I think we got wrong, and it's the piece I've spent much of the last ten years trying to repair.

r001.rationale: The response says expert systems gave advice, “which is a kind of action,” but does not explain that framing them solely as providers of correct answers let researchers disregard their agent status.

r002.rationale: It discusses agents’ objectives generally, but does not state that a question-answering system needs to reason about its own objectives.

r003.rationale: It mentions the consequences of agents’ actions in general, but does not say that giving an answer should be considered an action with effects.

astra-6.text:
I think the agent perspective was largely missing from the way we organized AI research in the 1980s. We had subfields—learning, planning, vision, natural language—and each tended to develop its own problems and measures of progress. But there wasn’t enough emphasis on how those pieces fitted together into a system that perceived an environment and acted in it.

Of course, the idea wasn’t new. The early ambition of AI was to build intelligent systems. But as the field became more specialized, we sometimes lost sight of the question: what makes an action intelligent? You can’t really answer that just by looking at an inference algorithm or a pattern recognizer in isolation. You need to consider what the system is trying to achieve, what it knows, and how its choices affect the world.

For me, the agent perspective provided a way to bring those questions back together. Learning and reasoning are capabilities that help an agent decide what to do. They’re not, by themselves, the definition of intelligence.

r001.rationale: The response says AI research became divided into subfields and lost focus on agents, but does not discuss expert systems being treated as providers of correct answers or researchers disregarding their agent status.

r002.rationale: It says systems need to consider what they are trying to achieve, but does not state that a question-answering system must reason about its own objectives.

r003.rationale: It discusses choices affecting the world in general, but does not say that giving an answer has effects as an action.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we had a somewhat fragmented view. People worked on search, planning, reasoning, learning, and perception, but often without asking how those pieces fitted together into a system that actually did something in the world. The agent perspective gives you a common framework: a system receives information from its environment and chooses actions, and then you ask what would make those actions intelligent.

That connects AI to the idea of rational decision-making. What an agent should do depends on its objectives, what it has observed, and what it knows about how the world works. A logical inference or a plan is useful insofar as it helps the agent choose an appropriate action; it isn’t necessarily an end in itself.

Of course, the idea wasn’t entirely new in the 1980s. But I felt we needed to make it much more explicit as an organizing principle for the field, rather than treating intelligence as a collection of separate technical problems.

r001.rationale: The response describes AI work as fragmented and promotes an agent framework, but it does not discuss expert systems or say that treating them as answer providers let researchers disregard their agency.

r002.rationale: It says actions depend on objectives, but does not state that a question-answering system needs to reason about its own objectives.

r003.rationale: It describes agents as choosing actions, but does not identify giving an answer as an action or discuss its effects.
